newsitem.title: JORDAN: U.S. delivers military transport plane to Jordan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. delivers military transport plane to Jordan.

text.p: Jordan formally took delivery of a long-range military transport plane from the United States on Tuesday, part of Washington's $300 million military aid package aimed at bolstering the ageing armed forces of a key Arab ally.

The arrival of the Lockheed C-130H aircraft, flown in from Utah, followed the handover of tanks, helicopters, trucks and naval vessels late last year after President Bill Clinton declared Jordan a major non-NATO ally of the United States.
The centrepiece of the military modernisation deal, 16 F-16 fighter bombers, is due to be delivered by February next year.

"The security of the Hashemite kingdom (of Jordan) and the security and prosperity of the people of Jordan are important objectives of ours," U.S. Ambassador Wesley Egan told a news conference inside a hangar at Amman's Marka airport.

The United States says it is helping revamp Jordan's armed forces in recognition of its new role in the Middle East after King Hussein signed a 1994 peace treaty with Israel and turned against his former ally Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.

Diplomats say that restocking Jordan's depleted military equipment will also boost morale among the kingdom's armed forces, a bedrock of support for the monarchy throughout King Hussein's 44-year rule.
The sums involved are modest compared to the billions of dollars in military assistance Washington pumps every year into Egypt and Israel, its other main allies in the region.
Egan said the aid package was an "exceptional step" that could not be repeated on an annual basis, but that Washington would continue to look for "creative" ways to support Jordan.
Last November Clinton named Jordan a major non-NATO ally of the United States, entitling it to priority consideration for military aid and equipment.
Jordan, sensitive to criticism that its closer ties to Washington could make it appear to be a U.S. stooge in the region, has stressed it retains full independence in military decisions.

"The (non-NATO) alliance means Jordan has access to U.S. arms, but there are no commitments," one army officer said on Tuesday. "We won't have to be a base for the U.S. to bomb Iraq like (NATO member) Turkey in the Gulf War."

U.S. pilots based in Jordan last year flew observation flights monitoring the Western-imposed no-fly zone in southern Iraq. But Jordan said it would not permit any aggressive action against Iraq to be launched from its territory.
"Our military policy is purely defensive," Air Force Chief of Staff Major-General Mohammad Ababneh said when asked if Jordan focused its forces on its eastern or western borders.
"We just want to make sure (an aggressor) would have to stop to think not once, but two or three times about it," he said.
Ababneh said the U.S. supplies would "strengthen the friendly cooperation between our two countries", but he said that Jordan's needs were still a long way from being met.

"This is our fifth (C-130) plane. We hope for more, and we need more," he told the news conference. "We will ask for additional F-16s from the United States to increase our number of planes and to replace older ones."
He said the two countries planned joint air and land training exercises at the start of next month featuring helicopters and fighter jets from both sides.
"This continued cooperation will not only enhance our strengths and capabilities but will lead to a brighter, more prosperous future for our airforce," Ababneh said.
